title: Morus: freedom for civic virtue is God's gift, not nature's
source_text: VIII. Quibus consentanea sunt quae docet Alexander Morus jam citata Disputatione. Porro, inquit, libertas illa, qua leges condunt, Rempublicam temperant, in commune consulunt, victorias reportant, & virtutibus variis praelucent, etiam ii qui versantur in statu peccati, non ita locum habet in iis, quasi ex ipsius naturae incunabulis existeret. A Deo enim est luminum Patre, a quo donum omne bonum descendit, quod illi ipsi agnoverunt, quum neminem virum insignem oriri absque divino afflatu scribunt: & ratio ipsa persuadebat: cur enim Heroum filii tam degeneres, cur eodem partu editi tam dissimiles occurrerent? cur educatione optima imbuti immanes belluae fierent? thesi quadragesima sexta. Quibus thesi sequenti subjicit, Nempe Dei provida manus in ipso exortu probae indolis quaedam veluti semina spargit, ac deinde culturae opportunitates objicit, quae tamen parum prodessent, nisi hominum nequitiae Deus spiritus sui habenis moderaretur: nam cum velit humanam societatem ordine legitimo contineri, omnium pariter ferocire proterviam non sinit, sed alios metu poenae compescit, alios amore praemii accendit: alioqui summa rerum esset confusio, si quam proni sunt omnes ad mala omne genus, tam in ea prorumperent.
pass_a_gloss: VIII. With which agree the things which Alexander Morus teaches in the Disputation already cited. Moreover, he says, that liberty by which they make laws, temper the Commonwealth, consult for the common good, carry off victories, and shine forth in various virtues, even those who are in the state of sin, does not so have place in them, as if from the very cradle of nature it existed. For it is from God the Father of lights, from whom every good gift descends, which they themselves acknowledged, when they write that no man distinguished arises without divine inspiration: and reason itself persuaded: for why should the sons of Heroes so degenerate, why should those born of the same birth meet us so unlike? why should those imbued with the best education become savage beasts? thesis forty-sixth. To which in the following thesis he subjoins, Namely the provident hand of God in the very birth of a good disposition scatters as it were certain seeds, and then throws in opportunities of cultivation, which however would profit little, unless God moderated the wickedness of men with the reins of his spirit: for since he wills human society to be held in lawful order, he does not allow the wantonness of all alike to run wild, but some by fear of punishment he restrains, others by love of reward he kindles: otherwise there would be the utmost confusion of things, if, as prone as all are to evils of every kind, so far they burst forth into them.
pass_b_english: Thesis VIII. What Alexander Morus teaches in the disputation already cited agrees with this. 'Further,' he says, 'the liberty by which men make laws, govern the state, take counsel for the common good, win victories and shine in various virtues, even those who live in the state of sin, is not present in them as if it arose from the very cradle of nature. It comes from God, the Father of lights, from whom every good gift comes down. They acknowledged this themselves when they wrote that no distinguished man arises without divine inspiration, and reason itself convinced them. Otherwise why would the sons of heroes so degenerate, why would twins born together turn out so unlike, and why would men trained in the best education become savage beasts?' (thesis 46).

In the next thesis he adds: 'God's provident hand scatters, as it were, certain seeds of a good disposition at a man's very birth, and then puts opportunities for cultivating them in his way. These would do little good, though, unless God curbed men's wickedness with the reins of his Spirit. Since he wills that human society be held together in lawful order, he does not let everyone's insolence run wild alike, but restrains some by fear of punishment and kindles others by love of reward. Otherwise everything would be in utter confusion, if men broke out into evils of every kind as far as they are all inclined to them.'

choices.why: Morus echoes Cicero's dictum (De natura deorum 2.167) that no great man was ever without some divine afflatus; 'inspiration' keeps the classical sense.
